 USDA Proposes Efforts to Boost EBT Card Security
 A long-awaited proposal is a positive step forward, but could also push food assistant costs to states already facing new budgetary challenges due to the One Big Beautiful Bill. 
 By Rebekah Alvey

 --> October 21, 2026 – The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) released a proposed rule on Wednesday aimed at protecting recipients of federal food assistance from benefit theft , but without federal funds it could push more costs to states at an already precarious time.

 The new rule would require all states to convert Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards to a chip-system within two years of a final rule.
 Individuals receiving benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) use EBT cards at grocery stores. But those cards still use a magnetic strip, rather than the chip technology that most debit and credit cards have transitioned to.
 As a result, EBT cards have remained vulnerable to “skimming,” the process where a criminal can install a device on a card reader and steal a shopper’s card information. Criminals can then use that information to steal benefits, and SNAP recipients are often unable to get those dollars back.
 This is one of the largest forms of fraud and theft happening in the program, and an estimated $600 million was stolen from SNAP households in 2025. The issue began escalating four years ago, and as a result some states have taken it upon themselves to transition to chip-card technology.
 Justin King, policy director at Propel, an app that allows SNAP households to manage their EBT cards, called the proposal “welcome news.”
 “Households that rely on SNAP and EBT are already vulnerable; they need and deserve strong protections, no matter where they live,” King said in an email. “There’s more work to be done, but this is a big step forward.”
 Currently, eight states have adopted chip card technology with another six enrolled in a pilot project. Under the Biden administration, the USDA finalized a standard for EBT chip technology, which propelled the number of states moving to this technology.
 But the transition to chip technology is not cheap. The proposed rule estimates it will cost $283 million in upfront costs for state agencies, the federal government, households and businesses.
 “This is an unfunded mandate,” Gina Plata-Nino, SNAP director at the Food Research and Action Center, said of the proposal. “It’s not realistic for states to be able to do this.”
 We’ll bring the news to you.

 Sign up today Sign up today Already, state budgets are under strain from additional costs included in the Republican’s One Big Beautiful Bill . Historically, the state and federal government split administrative costs of SNAP —like transitioning systems to chipped-EBT cards. Now under the OBBB, states are responsible for 75 percent of the administrative costs, an additional millions of dollars for most states.
 State leaders are also worried about upcoming costs for SNAP benefits. For the first time, the OBBB mandates that some states cover a portion of benefits, with the full amount dependent on the state’s SNAP payment error rate.
 Ahead of this proposal, some state officials told ProPublica they paused chip-card implementation due to the new costs and policies under the OBBB. Plata-Nino said some states quickly rolled out their chip cards ahead of the administrative cost shift kicking in.
 Already, Plata-Nino said some states are considering pulling out of SNAP or pausing it because they can’t afford the benefit cost-shift.
 “How are they going to have the money to implement something that is needed, but right now cannot be a priority?” Plata-Nino said.
 Lawmakers have meanwhile introduced bills to help fund the transition to chip cards, but those have moved with little success. ( Link to this post .)
